title: Resume vs CV: They Are Not the Same
excerpt: A resume is short and targeted. A CV is comprehensive and documents your academic journey. Here is the difference and which one you actually need.

blocks.text: Resume vs CV: They Are Not the Same! 🎓

Before we get into how to write an academic resume, we need to clear up a common misunderstanding. In many places Resume and CV are used in place of each other, but conceptually, especially in Academic Applications, these two are not the same.
What Is a Resume?
A Resume is a short, condensed, and targeted document that is not supposed to display your entire academic and professional background. Its goal is to say in one look:
"Who I am, what skills and experience I have, and why I'm suitable for this position."
So a Resume is usually Position-Oriented or Job-Oriented; meaning it's written and Tailored for a specific position.
For example, if you're applying for a Machine Learning Engineer position, you should highlight ML projects, Python experience, and relevant Internships; not everything you did during your studies.
So the important principle of a Resume is:
Relevance over Completeness
A Resume is usually around 1 to 2 pages, but this is not an absolute rule and depends on the position, country, and the person's background.
What Is a CV?
CV stands for Curriculum Vitae and has a different philosophy.
A CV is more Comprehensive and its goal is to show your academic and professional path:
"What have I done in my academic and research path up to today?"
That's why it becomes more important in Academic Applications.
For example, for a PhD Position, a Professor might want to see your Research Experience, Publications, Thesis, Projects, Teaching Experience, Awards, Technical Skills, and Research Interests.
Here a short Resume usually can't present a complete picture of your Research Profile; so the Academic CV becomes important.
The Main Difference
If I want to say it very simply:
A Resume is a Selective and Targeted document of your most important experiences.
A CV is a Comprehensive document of your academic and professional path.
In a Resume the main question is:
"What things should I show for this position?"
But in a CV the main question is:
"What has my academic and professional path been up to today?"
Is This Difference the Same in All Countries?
No.
The meaning of CV and Resume can differ in different countries.
For example in America usually: Resume → shorter and more targeted CV → more comprehensive and more for Academic / Research Positions
But in many European countries, the word CV might be used for a short employment document too.
So don't just pay attention to the name CV or Resume; always check the Context and Application Instructions.
Which One Do We Want for a PhD?
If you're applying for positions like:
Usually an Academic CV is more suitable.
Because a Professor doesn't just want to know:
"What Skills does this person have?"
Rather they want to understand:
"What academic path has this person taken and what Research Potential do they have?"
An Academic CV Is Not Just a List
A common mistake is thinking:
"I dump everything I have into Word, so I have a CV."
No!

A good Academic CV must have an Academic Narrative; meaning when the Professor reads it, they can follow your path: Education → Research Experience → Publications → Projects → Teaching → Awards → Skills
So a CV is not just a list; it's a Structured Representation of Your Academic Journey.
A CV Is a Living Document
A Resume is usually re-Tailored for each Position. But an Academic CV is more like a Master Document that grows over time.
New paper → added. Conference → added. Research Project → added. Teaching Experience → added. Award → added.
So an Academic CV is a Living Document. Of course a longer CV is not necessarily better. Its length should be a function of the amount of Relevant Academic Content, not a specific number.
A Simple Mental Model
If I want to keep these two very simple in your mind:
Resume
"Why am I a good fit for this specific opportunity?"
Academic CV
"What have I done throughout my academic and research journey?"
An Important Mistake in PhD Applications
A person might have an excellent two-page Resume for a company and send the exact same file to a Professor.
In a company Resume the main focus might be on: Python, SQL, Docker, Git, FastAPI, Machine Learning
But for a PhD, if Research Experience, Publications, Thesis, Research Interests, and Academic Projects don't exist, you're practically introducing yourself with the wrong criteria.
Golden Rule 🎯
Before you write a CV or Resume, first ask this question:
Who is going to read this document, and what decision do they need to make?
If a Recruiter is going to read it, focus more on: Skills → Experience → Impact
If a Professor is going to read it, the focus should be more on: Research → Publications → Academic Experience → Technical Depth → Research Potential
So building a CV doesn't start with choosing a font and color!
It starts with this question:
What is the goal of this document and who is going to read it?
And in the end:
A good CV is not necessarily a long CV; it is a CV that presents the right information, with the right structure, to the right reader. 🎯
